prompt: A queue implemented as a fixed-size array without wraparound has what problem?
options: It runs out of usable space even when logically not full, as front/rear only advance forward
It cannot store more than 1 element
explanation: Without treating the array as cyclic (via modulo), the front/rear indices only ever increase, eventually running off the end even though slots at the beginning are free.

prompt: What operator makes a cyclic-array queue implementation work?
explanation: The modulo operator wraps the index back to 0 once it passes the end of the array.

prompt: [Real 2025 exam question] Which statement about stacks and queues is correct?
options: The stack and the queue both work by the LIFO principle.
The stack and the queue both work by the FIFO principle.
The stack works by LIFO, the queue by FIFO.
The stack works by FIFO, the queue by LIFO.

prompt: [Real 2025 exam question] Which two statements about stacks/queues are correct?
options: An element in the middle of a stack can be accessed without removing the elements above it.
Push and pop on a stack typically run in O(1).
Enqueue and dequeue on a queue typically run in O(n).
Enqueueing then immediately dequeueing on a queue returns the same element only if the queue was empty beforehand.
explanation: Push/pop are O(1) with a proper array or linked implementation. If the queue wasn't empty, dequeue returns whatever was already at the front, not the just-enqueued element — only an empty queue guarantees enqueue then dequeue returns the same element.

prompt: Implementing a Queue with two Stacks (S1, S2): dequeue() checks if S2 is empty, and if so drains all of S1 into S2 first. Why does this drain step correctly reverse the order?
options: Popping every element off S1 (LIFO) and pushing each onto S2 (LIFO) inverts the order twice-removed, putting the oldest enqueued element on top of S2
It doesn't reverse anything -- S2 ends up in the same order as S1
The drain step is only needed to free memory, not to fix ordering
Stacks cannot be drained into each other without a queue as intermediate storage
explanation: S1 has the oldest enqueued element at the BOTTOM (pushed first). Popping S1 (removes from top, i.e. newest first) and pushing onto S2 reverses that order, so the oldest element ends up on TOP of S2 -- exactly where a dequeue (pop) needs it.

prompt: Implementing a Stack with two Queues, pop() must reach the most-recently-pushed element. What is the worst-case time complexity of a single pop() call?
explanation: Since a queue can only dequeue from the front, reaching the last-pushed element requires shuffling every other element into the second queue first -- O(n).
